action_criteria.expected_evidence: Active denervation with chronic neurogenic change confined to the right cervical region; complex fasciculation potentials in cervical, lumbosacral and thoracic muscles without fibrillations outside the cervical region; normal motor conduction without block; normal sensory studies.
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal brain MRI: no structural, vascular, demyelinating or neoplastic lesion and no corticospinal tract signal change.
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude structural, vascular, demyelinating, inflammatory or neoplastic causes of the upper motor neuron or bulbar signs
action_criteria.rationale: MRI does not confirm ALS. It excludes brain and brainstem lesions that can cause upper motor neuron or bulbar signs; corticospinal tract signal change, when present, is supportive only.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Mild C3-C6 degenerative changes with mild right C5-C6 foraminal narrowing; no canal stenosis, cord compression or cord signal change.
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI of the cervical and thoracic cord, and of the lumbosacral spine when lower limb signs need it, to exclude compressive myelopathy, radiculopathy and other cord lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy is the commonest structural mimic of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs in the limbs. Spine MRI excludes it, but incidental spondylosis does not explain bulbar signs or denervation in other regions and must not delay the ALS work-up.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: CK 312 U/L (1.8x ULN); blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function, B12, folate, ESR and CRP normal.
action_criteria.label: Blood tests for treatable mimics and a pre-treatment baseline: full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes and calcium, CK, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, ESR and CRP
action_criteria.rationale: These tests exclude metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory mimics and give the liver and blood-count baseline needed before riluzole; phenotype-specific tests are added only when the case raises that mimic.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 86% predicted and SNIP 82 cmH2O, within normal limits: baseline for 3-monthly monitoring.
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP, with MIP where available) to stage respiratory muscle involvement and plan monitoring and NIV
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function does not diagnose ALS. Once ALS is supported it stages respiratory muscle weakness, sets the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring and identifies patients who need early referral for NIV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic C9orf72 expansion and no pathogenic variant in SOD1, TARDBP, FUS or TBK1; a negative result does not exclude ALS.
action_criteria.label: ALS gene panel (C9orf72 repeat expansion; SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1) after pre-test genetic counselling, once the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment is complete
action_criteria.rationale: Genetic testing does not make the diagnosis. It is offered with counselling to people with ALS because a pathogenic variant changes counselling for relatives and may open gene-targeted treatment or trials.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Buspirone and amlodipine do not interact with riluzole; baseline and scheduled transaminase monitoring.
action_criteria.label: Check riluzole against the current medicines, alcohol use and liver function before the first dose, once the diagnosis is established
action_criteria.rationale: Riluzole is metabolised by CYP1A2 and can raise liver transaminases, so the medicine list, alcohol use and baseline liver function are reviewed before treatment. No current medicine interacts with it. The Gold Coast criteria are met, so riluzole is started at this visit.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not reassure him on the basis of the earlier benign fasciculation syndrome diagnosis: new weakness, wasting, upper motor neuron signs and denervation override it.

Do not refer for cervical spine surgery on the basis of the mild right C5-C6 foraminal narrowing: it does not explain the denervation in C8-T1 hand muscles, the upper motor neuron signs or the widespread complex fasciculations.
Do not attribute the progressive weakness or wasting to anxiety or a functional disorder.
Do not treat ALS with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange: they have no benefit.
required_recommendations: Make and explain the diagnosis of ALS by Gold Coast 2020 criteria: progressive right arm weakness and wasting with upper motor neuron signs (right Hoffman sign, brisk biceps and brachioradialis reflexes) and lower motor neuron involvement in the cervical region on examination and EMG (active and chronic denervation), with complex fasciculations elsewhere and mimics excluded by MRI and blood tests; disclose it in a planned face-to-face discussion, acknowledging the earlier benign fasciculation diagnosis.
Review in about 3 months with repeat examination, and repeat EMG/NCS if needed to document spread beyond the cervical region.

Repeat FVC and SNIP about every 3 months and ask at each review about orthopnoea, morning headache, daytime sleepiness and unrefreshing sleep, referring for NIV assessment when these appear or values fall.

Offer riluzole 50 mg twice daily. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x the upper limit of normal, and ask the patient to report any febrile illness so that neutropenia can be excluded.
Refer to the specialist ALS clinic for follow-up and multidisciplinary support.
Offer genetic counselling and, if the patient wishes, ALS genetic testing, explaining the implications for relatives.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

accepted: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), early limb-onset, Gold Coast criteria met (possible ALS by Awaji criteria)

differential.key_features: supports: earlier BFS label after a normal EMG 2 years ago, long-standing fasciculations; against: new weakness and wasting, a new right Hoffman sign and brisk reflexes, active and chronic denervation in the right arm, complex fasciculations

key_clinical_evidence: Gold Coast 2020 accepts upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in one body region, which the right arm meets here (right Hoffman sign and brisk reflexes with active and chronic denervation); by Awaji 2008 the findings are possible ALS because electrodiagnostic lower motor neuron evidence is confined to the cervical region. The earlier benign label does not stand: Gold Coast is met now, and a repeat EMG documents spread but is not needed to make the diagnosis.
EMG lower motor neuron evidence is chronic neurogenic change with active denervation; by Awaji 2008 fasciculation potentials count as active denervation in a muscle with chronic neurogenic change.
Complex fasciculations raise concern for motor neuron disease but are not diagnostic alone; here they accompany weakness, wasting, upper motor neuron signs and chronic neurogenic change.
A normal EMG and a benign fasciculation syndrome label 2 years ago do not exclude later motor neuron disease; new weakness, wasting and upper motor neuron signs require reassessment.
Normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block argue against multifocal motor neuropathy, and normal sensory responses argue against a sensorimotor neuropathy or SBMA.
CK 312 U/L (1.8x ULN): mild to moderate elevation is common in ALS from denervation and does not by itself suggest a myopathy.

FVC 86% predicted and SNIP 82 cmH2O are normal at baseline. AAN 2009 markers that prompt NIV discussion are orthopnoea, FVC below 50% predicted, SNIP below 40 cmH2O, MIP weaker than -60 cmH2O or abnormal overnight oximetry; NIV prolongs survival and improves quality of life (Bourke 2006).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A benign fasciculation syndrome label based on a normal EMG 2 years ago does not exclude ALS; new weakness, wasting, an upper motor neuron sign and active plus chronic denervation mandate criteria-based reassessment and repeat EMG.
red_herrings.data_point: Prior diagnosis of benign fasciculation syndrome
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors current presentation as benign progression of BFS, deferring further workup

sequence_constraints.reason: Genetic testing follows the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment and pre-test counselling; it does not make the diagnosis.
Riluzole is considered only after the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment supports ALS.

specialized_test.impression: Active denervation (fibrillations +1, positive sharp waves +1) and chronic reinnervation (large amplitude, long duration MUPs, reduced recruitment) are present in the right cervical region. Complex fasciculation potentials are noted in multiple regions (cervical, lumbosacral, possible thoracic); morphologically long duration (>5ms), polyphasic, multiple turns. Sensory NCS entirely normal. Right median motor CMAP mildly reduced; conduction velocities normal; no conduction block. Findings indicate a localized disorder of anterior horn cells in the cervical region with widespread fasciculation activity

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. K is a 52-year-old software engineer who presents for reassessment after a previous diagnosis of benign fasciculation syndrome (BFS) made 2 years ago by another neurologist following a normal EMG at that time. He returns because his family has noticed new right arm weakness and visible wasting of his right hand over the past 6 months.

He has had widespread muscle twitching for over 2 years, initially confined to his calves and thighs, which were attributed to BFS after a normal EMG at an outside institution. He is extremely anxious about ALS given family members who have searched the internet. His prior neurologist reassured him extensively.

Over the past 6 months, however, new symptoms have emerged that he has minimized or rationalized: visible wasting of the right first dorsal interosseous muscle, difficulty holding a pen and typing with his right hand, and right hand cramping. He has also noticed right foot mild dragging when he runs but not clearly when walking slowly. He denies swallowing difficulties, speech changes, or sensory symptoms.

Examination today shows mild right thenar atrophy, right-sided weakness in deltoid and intrinsic muscles, and a new right Hoffman sign that was not documented in prior neurology notes. Plantar responses are equivocal.

neurological_exam.additional: Fasciculations visible in right arm and bilateral calves at rest. Prior diagnosis of benign fasciculation syndrome noted but exam today shows subtle new changes.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Tongue midline, no obvious atrophy. Possible sparse fasciculations on prolonged observation. No dysarthria. Jaw jerk normal to mildly increased.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Anxious. Minimizes symptoms citing prior benign fasciculation syndrome diagnosis.
neurological_exam.motor: Right arm: deltoid 4+/5, biceps 4+/5, intrinsic hand 4/5. Mild right thenar atrophy. Left arm: near full strength 4+/5 to 5/5. Lower extremities: mild right tibialis anterior weakness 4+/5. No obvious atrophy lower extremities.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 3+ bilaterally. Brachioradialis 3+ bilaterally. Knee jerks 3+ bilaterally. Ankle jerks 2+. Right Hoffman positive. Plantar responses equivocal bilaterally — NOT clearly extensor.
